utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody. The witness should be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Joseph. Welcome back to the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I remind you that the affirmation to tell the truth still applies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And Mr. Tolimir is continuing the cross-examination. Mr. Tolimir, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon to all. May there be peace in this house, and may God's will be done in these proceedings and not mine. Good afternoon to Mr. Joseph, I do wish him a comfortable stay among us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were discussing a document yesterday, you said that you wouldn't have an answer to that, so I'd like us to look at the statement of yours we reviewed yesterday, and let us see what you have to say about this problem in your statement. I'll direct you to the exact page. That's 65 ter 07203, but I was looking to see if there's a different number now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is now D173.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have D173 shown in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We don't have it on the screen yet.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We'll read from paragraph 3 because the statement has numbered paragraphs. That's page 2, paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Where you state that: "In the second half of July of 1995, I was acting as a civil affairs officer for UNPROFOR in Tuzla, where I was helping the incoming refugees from Srebrenica. Probably due to my experiences with the refugees, I was called to Sarajevo to prepare a possible mission to Zepa, where an evacuation of a large number of civilians was expected." You say "in the second half of July." Can you tell us precisely which date that was? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon as well to the accused and to Mr. Gajic. And thank you for the good wishes. And to answer this question, the date would have been on or about the 11th of July, 1995. And if I could add, to the Chamber, in the interests of clarifying things as this very well may be my last day of testimony, the accused mentioned a reluctance on my part to speak to prior documents. And I would just like to inform the Chamber and the accused and his attorney that if -- to really put this question to rest: If the accused would like me to stipulate that the Armija had weapons in Zepa, I'm willing to stipulate that. Further, if the accused would like me to stipulate that in safe areas the Armija conducted military operations from them in general, I'm willing to stipulate that too. And, third, I'm willing to stipulate that this was a major preoccupation for the Serbs. I'll willing to stipulate to all three of those. What I'm not able to do for this Chamber, unfortunately, is go over intercepts and specific communication and interpret and analyse those, as I really at the time had no specific information about the nature of military activities inside and from within the safe area at the time. And I just felt that that might be helpful to the Chamber and to the accused as well, if I could just put that out there. Thank you all very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And I apologise if I was vague. We had a document, that we'll go back to after we've dealt with this, which is perhaps even more important for Their Honours than for you or I. We know how the events unfolded; they don't. That's why I was referring to the chronology of these events. This was for the benefit of the Chamber. But I do accept your explanation and interpretation. Please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, before you continue with your next question, Judge Mindua has a question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, good afternoon to you, sir. I'd like to go back to what you've just said, in fact. On the transcript, page 2 and 3, you stated that you can affirm and state that the Armija had weapons in Zepa. You also said that you can state that the Armija did carry out military operations, generally speaking, from Zepa. But in fact, you were in charge of civilian affairs there in Zepa. So what is your basis in order to state that there were weapons and military operations? Did you carry out investigations about that or were you privy to some information about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I thank the Judge for this important opportunity to clarify. I think this is very important for me to be precise. When I spoke, I chose my words carefully and I hope they were accurately rendered in translation. I said that we -- I was willing to affirm or stipulate that the Armija had weapons in Zepa. And the basis for this is, even if I can recall, I believe, if memory serves, that Colonel Palic, for example, had a side-arm. And I believe it was generally understood, although we did not conduct any survey, it was understood that the Armija had weapons. So the basis -- to answer your question, Your Honour, it would be generally on the basis of widely-accepted information in UNPROFOR that there were weapons, that the Armija had weapons. With respect to military operations, I chose my words very carefully. I said I was willing to attest that in general there were military operations conducted from safe areas. I did not say, and certainly did not intend to say, from Zepa in particular because I precisely, Your Honour - and this is why I thank you for the opportunity to clarify - because I did not have the specific information either in the immediate run-up to these events or prior, what the Armija was actually doing in Zepa. And here I should add there were different stories. There's a narrative, an accepted narrative, about Srebrenica that Naser Oric was quite active. I'm not a fact witness to that but that was a narrative that there was. And there was a narrative that Commander Palic was rather more calm and quiescent. But I cannot provide and shed light on that specific information, and that would be better, I believe, for General Smith. But I was saying, in general, were we aware that safe areas were at times used for military operations; the answer is, yes. And as I mentioned yesterday for the accused, I was in another safe area, Bihac, which was the site of a rather sizeable attack by a Armija commander there - his name was Dudakovic, in Bihac - and he went on a quite significant attack in Serb forces, as General Tolimir well remembers, and so I'm well aware that such events could transpire. But I cannot for this Chamber give specific information about what Colonel Palic and his forces were doing and the nature of any operations that they might have conducted or might not have. And it was for that reason I was explaining for the accused my reluctance to give commentary and analysis and be responding to intercepts that they had. I just felt it was important for the Court and all present to understand the nature of that reluctance. I hope that answers your question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: For the clarity of the transcript, I would like to ask you: When you refer to -- when you use the word "Armija," are you referring to the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. That is correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you. Mr. Tolimir, please, now your next question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Joseph, so you arrived on the 11th and before your arrival there, you attended a briefing with David Harland, senior officer for civilian affairs, and General Rupert Smith. And this is something that you stated in paragraph 4 of your statement that we have before us. Can you tell us, were you given any sort of tasks from them in relation to the Armija, or did they only have to do with the civilian population in Zepa? When I say the "Armija," the BH army, I mean the units present in Zepa.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had only the most general instructions, and we had no specific instruction to conduct a certain activity with the Armija, nor did we have any instruction to refrain from engaging with elements of the Armija or to refrain from any activity with them. It was very, very general. What we knew was, operating on the information that we had at the time, A, this was a crisis underscored by what had just transpired in Srebrenica and with this mass exodus and with some serious allegations of crimes like rapes and disappearances of -- during the transport. So that was the first thing that we had on our mind. And then it was to focus on the evacuation, as I said, of the women and children first and, should an agreement be reached, then the men of Zepa. So that's the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Joseph. Did General Smith tell you at the time anything about the UN policy in relation to the enclaves, because by that time he would have received the document we discussed yesterday, the one you said you may have seen at the time or not? I don't know if you know which I'm referring -- one I'm referring to. That's the one sent by Mr. Akashi to Mr. Annan and which was copied to Mr. Smith on the 11th of July. Did he tell you anything about the UNPROFOR policy towards the enclaves, since he was sending you on a mission that had to do with refugees? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had a general understanding about our policy and, more important, our mandate with respect to the enclaves, but I would have to ask the accused to be more specific about a specific policy contained in that report that he is referring to so that I can answer whether or not we were aware of that. I would need to know specifically what policy the accused is speaking of.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll quote a line from the report we saw yesterday, and that will help to refresh your memory. It's a line from the letter sent by Mr. Akashi to Mr. Annan and Rupert Smith. And in line one, it says: "What sort of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, we don't have that on the screen. It's helpful for everybody. This is D174. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You see the document there, and I'll be reading from paragraph 1. It's actually line 5. "A general consensus was reached on the policy that UNPF, UNPROFOR, and UNHCR will pursue with regard to Srebrenica in the coming one to seven days, depending on the evolution of events on the ground, the stance taken by the parties, and the attitude of the people living in Srebrenica." Thank you. This is my question: Bearing in mind that the letter sent by Mr. Akashi had already reached the addressees by that time and that on the 11th it was already apparent that Srebrenica had been placed under the control of the VRS and that the Muslim population had started moving out, my question was if he had given you any sort of instructions in view of this? He was sending you to Zepa to attend to the refugees there, and it was in the context of this policy that my question was formulated. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm still not seeing the specific policy in the communique, the message sent by Mr. Akashi, that would bear on us. Were we generally aware? And we might well have specifically been aware. As I said, I might well have seen this document. I don't recall anything in particular, but we might well have been aware of evolving policy. We should have been aware of evolving policy. But I don't see a specific policy point here about what we should or should not do, and that's why I can't be more precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's look at page 2 of the document. That's something we looked at yesterday. And in order not to go through the entire document, let's just look at the last sentence in the Serbian language, which reads -- so the last sentence on page 2 in the Serbian version, which reads: "UNPROFOR with the support of UNHCR will also endeavour to reach agreement," on page 3, "with the Bosnian Serbs to escort any convoy of refugees from Srebrenica to Tuzla." Thank you. In view of this and in view of what I've said before, you must have received instructions in line with this, since you were dispatched to receive refugees there. That's what I meant when I said that UNPROFOR must have had a policy by the 11th with regard to the refugees. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very useful that you mentioned 11th because that is when Srebrenica would have fallen. That was on or about the 11th when it would have fallen. And whatever policy was agreed there on the 11th, it's very important to know, yes, we would have had that in our minds but we would also have had subsequent experience with -- after the fall of Srebrenica, after the 11th, with what happened with those who were moved out of Srebrenica and received in Tuzla, in the Tuzla area. And those dynamics were probably more forefront on our minds than what was contained here or whatever, in general, principle is contained here. So I hope I've addressed your question, General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's go back to your statement. We don't need this document anymore. Your statement is D173, paragraph 4, where you say that you were at a meeting with David Harland, civil affairs senior officer, and General Rupert Smith, UNPROFOR commander for the BH. That's in lines 1 through 3 of paragraph 4. Tell me now, what was it that General Smith told you specifically before you set out for Tuzla where he dispatched you? Thank you. Of course, if you can remember. I want you to speak in general terms. You don't need to give me the specific tasks. Or was it just him telling you that you should go there? I apologise, perhaps your dilemma might be down to the fact that we are still speaking about Srebrenica and that's to say before you were sent to Zepa and what was it that he told you about it, about the policy; that was my question.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was sent to Tuzla from direction of UNPROFOR headquarters in Zagreb, not from Sarajevo and General Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. It was for this reason that I was reading this document to you, D174, because those were guide-lines sent from Zagreb on the 11th of July. But if you can tell us, what were the specific tasks that you received in Tuzla in relation to Srebrenica? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The specific mission was to work with UNPROFOR military and UNHCR and ICRC and any and all others to as best as possible receive, accommodate, and deal with this influx of something on the order of 20.000 displaced persons from -- who were pushed out of Srebrenica. That was the -- that was our challenge.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Joseph. Now we are in Tuzla and you were there to receive refugees from Srebrenica who were arriving in Tuzla, crossing the Serb territory. Can you tell us what -- whatever you can recall and whether you did actually receive a large number of refugees who were getting there on buses?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer to the second question is, yes, absolutely. We received bus after bus of persons from Srebrenica, primarily or almost exclusively women and children - using the term displaced persons because you know refugees is a term under international law where they cross an international border and this was not an international border - and so we were absolutely swamped to take care of these persons who had been pushed out of their homes in Srebrenica and now we had to accommodate them -- because they were no longer in their homes, we had to accommodate them on -- thousands of them on this airbase in Tuzla, and so we were working closely with UNPROFOR, military, UNHCR, and others to do just that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In view of that being so, did you send reports regarding the number of refugees that were received per day after all of the convoys had arrived and the convoys that had crossed Republika Srpska territory? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may well have sent reports to that effect. And presumably the Chamber and the Prosecution and accused have copies, if those reports exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, we will show you again 1D28 that I wanted to discuss yesterday, where we can see a reference to what I was asking you about. And perhaps then it will be easier to get an answer from you about what the situation was there and what the situation in Srebrenica was.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now can we please have 1D28 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This document is entitled, "The Chronology of Events, The Breakthrough of the 28th Division of the Land Forces," and this was the title that was given to this communication by whoever authored this text. We see that this was sent by the Commander Delic, and it was --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: It was sent to Commander Delic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now can we see page 4 which will discuss the events that you were involved in. Can we have page 4. In English that will be page 5. Thank you to Aleksandar for reminding me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think with this document there are some confusions with the names. It was sent by a certain Delic to a certain Delic. It disappeared now from the screen, we saw it and this was the -- it was sent by Commander Delic to Rasim Delic, if I'm not mistaken. Two different persons with the same name. Mr. Gajic, and then we should have it again, the first page, I think it will help us. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it is clear from the first page, and we have it now, that this document was sent by the Commander Brigadier Sead Delic to General Rasim Delic. These are two distinct individuals and they are on different positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed, indeed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And their last name is the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed. Both are commanders of different units with a different rank and different first name but the same family name. I think that is now clear on the record. Please continue, Mr. Tolimir, and we should look at the second page, as you requested. Page 5.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I requested page 4 in Serbian and page 5 in English. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now, we see here some of the tasks that you had within your mission there. And let's see the part that relates to your mission there, to do with the civil population, because that was the reason why you were in Tuzla. Now, if we look at the third paragraph, we can see there it reads as follows: "The first groups of people expelled from Srebrenica arrived in the Kladanj Sector at about 2100 hours on the 12th of July, 1995, and the majority of them, on July 13th, 1995, the majority of them, some 22.000 to 23.000 people, came to the general sector of Dubrava airport in the early morning and daring the day, while some came via the Baljkovica-Sapna corridor. A total of 29.336 persons expelled from the enclave," and I stress 29.336 persons, "were accommodated according to the list provided by municipalities. And then he goes on to list the various towns and places as the people reported, Lukavac, Banovici, Srebrenik, Gradacac, Zivinice, Kladanj, and so on. Now, the list that you have of the number of displaced persons, was it actually consistent with the number that we see here? Or were the numbers different, because you were supposed to receive your information from them? Or was it the case that you in fact registered them independently? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: To answer this question, I can't at this time state whether the statistics in this report which is a internal communication of the -- in the Armija - and not for that reason; it doesn't matter if it were a internal Serb communication - I can't at this time speak to the accuracy or any lack of accuracy about the statistics. So that's my answer to the question. And just if the Chamber please, I might be able to just eliminate any confusion about the Delics. Perhaps it would make it easier for the Chamber. Rasim Delic was the overall commander. His predecessor was Sefer Halilovic, who was mentioned in one of the documents that General Tolimir had mentioned. So Rasim Delic was -- and we knew him to be the overall commander of the Armija.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Joseph. You said internal Serb documents, however, these are Muslim documents and that's why we read out from it and we read the names of the person sending and to whom he was sending. But while we still have this page before us, I would like the Trial Chamber to look at the numbers and the paragraph below the place names that are listed there and the number of refugees, and we will see that it refers to the events that both you and I were eye-witnesses to. And I will now read from it: "The commander of the 28th Division of the KoV, who spent the last few months in Tuzla with a group of officers, left on the afternoon of the 13th of July, 1995, together with the PK, assistant commander for intelligence of the 28th Division, M Semso; desk officer for the PVO 2nd Corps, K Sabic, and several other officers from the 28th Division of the land forces command for the Medjedja-Nezuk Sector to try to establish radio communication with the units of the 28th Division of the land forces who had set out in the direction of Tuzla." And I end the quote there. Now my question is: Did the UNPROFOR know or did you personally know that some of the commanders who had been on a reconnaissance mission were already in Tuzla and that their job was in fact to link up these units? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Tolimir, I believe I -- I'm wait for the -- to be ready to hear my answer. I believe I testified just now rather clearly that our preoccupation was dealing with the influx of persons pushed out of Srebrenica because the VRS had entered there. And so this was not a preoccupation of mine. And so I cannot speak to what UNPROFOR was aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you get in touch with Naser Oric or any of his commanders while you were in Tuzla at the time when you were receiving and finding accommodation for the refugees? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, although we were in communication with UNPROFOR civilians in Srebrenica who -- they would be Bosniaks or Muslims, who were there and who were in quite some distress over whether they would be moved out with the Dutch UNPROFOR or be left behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell the Trial Chamber the following: Did the Dutch UNPROFOR unit in Srebrenica have information that commander Naser Oric and a group of command officers were in Tuzla in order to prepare the ground for linking up the detachment with Tuzla and that they had left Srebrenica two months before the fall of the enclave? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: This question and this line of inquiry is something that I cannot shed any light on, General Tolimir, because I simply do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you then answer the following question: How come that the commander of the 28th Division, Naser Oric, and his officers, Semso and the other, how come that they were in Tuzla? Because we can read here who were there in Tuzla before the enclave fell. Can you see that part? It's in the paragraph that I quoted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I haven't stood up so far on this line of questioning from this document, but I think the witness has been very patient trying to communicate that his knowledge of these events, specifically with respect to the Armija elements as depicted in this document, are beyond his knowledge. He's repeatedly tried to communicate that to the accused, and we have yet another question that's not even related to the words of the document but is now asking him about the intentions of the Armija commanders that are listed in the document. I mean, we're really wasting time with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, not to waste time, that was not the question. The only question was: "Can you see that part?" And: "... how come that they were in Tuzla? Because we can read here who were there in Tuzla before the enclave fell."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And that's the question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That's the question. And he said that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: -- how come they were in Tuzla. And he's repeatedly saying, I don't know anything about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, that's true, but I would like to hear the answer of the witness, if he can say and testify of that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I don't have useful information on that, on the presence of Mr. Oric in the Tuzla area prior to the fall of Srebrenica. I know later, afterwards, it was the subject of quite some lot of speculation and so forth. But, again, our focus was on dealing with this influx of persons displaced from Srebrenica, and this is not something that we focused on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, as always, it is helpful for your case to put questions to the witness he really can answer and to provide to us his knowledge about the events he personally witnessed. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Now, to go back to the first question. The first sentence of this paragraph we can read, the commander of the 28th Division of the lands forces who spent the last few months in Tuzla, and that's when I asked whether the UNPROFOR command in Srebrenica was aware of the fact that Naser Oric had left for Tuzla in order to prepare the ground for something. So I didn't ask whether the witness knew about this but whether the UNPROFOR command in Srebrenica knew about it, if he had any information in that respect. That was the gist of my question. Thank you. Can we now have 65 ter 7205 [Realtime transcript read in error "0275"]. This is a UN document dated the 15th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I would like to refer you to page 2, paragraph 5, which states that the BH police provided the following information regarding the number of persons and places. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you have used the document 1D28 with the witness. Are you going to tender it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to tender it because the Trial Chamber will -- it will be helpful to the Trial Chamber because it speaks to the events on this one page. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I didn't receive any specific answer of the witness in relation to this document; nevertheless, we will receive it as an exhibit. But that doesn't say anything about the reliability of the content of it. The Chamber will give weight to that at a later time.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And the document will be assigned D00176, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir, is the number correct, 65 ter 0275? I'm not sure if that is correct. This is recorded.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. It should be 65 ter 7205. And we will see that it speaks about the same data that we see in this document, and that is why I thought that this document would be helpful to jog the witness's memory, because it was in his report. Thank you. So 65 ter 7205. And my apologies, this is not Mr. Joseph's report, this is actually the UN -- a UN report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We can see that it is dated July 15th, 1995. And among others we can see that the third name from the bottom is Mr. David Harland's, who also was named in the report.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And could we see the page which -- page 2, paragraph 5, where we will see that there is a table.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And it says that information was gathered from individuals from the towns where the population from Srebrenica were going to. We can see that the numbers that appear here almost across the board are lower than the numbers we saw earlier. Here we see the number is 3.617 persons from Lukavac, whereas on the other document it was 3900 something. Then Srebrenik, it was 4.043, whereas here it's 3.505 for Srebrenik. So my question is this: Where does this discrepancy come from in the number of individuals that are recorded as having arrived from these locations to Tuzla? So where is -- where does this discrepancy come from between the reports that we have from the Armija and this report?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not have any basis to explain any discrepancy.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, tell us, please, who provided accommodation and who organised accommodations for the people who were arriving from Srebrenica on those buses? Was it you or was it the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those who were accommodated at the Tuzla airbase, it was generally UNHCR with intensive support from UNPROFOR. Those who were accommodated off the base, that is, in Tuzla and other locales, it would -- possibly there was some UNHCR support but possibly it might have been local authorities who had, and persons, just individual civilians, if they were accommodated in homes. But we -- our preoccupation was with the major influx which was directed towards the airbase, and we were quite overwhelmed to get them accommodated in the short time that it -- that it took for them to arrive at our door-step.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. They were also supposed to be taken care of in other ways. They were supposed to be fed and accommodated and so on. So did you -- or did you get from the UNHCR the exact number of individuals who had arrived from the Srebrenica enclave to Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to look at this report. And for the benefit of the accused, actually, I was the drafter of this report. It says that on the first page. I'd have to refresh my memory and look at the reports to find out what was the source of the information and what information UNHCR provided us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. The reason I put this question is that it says here that the police, the Bosnian police, provided this. However, this is not really too important. My next question is this: Can you tell the Trial Chamber what the total number of refugees that you received from the Srebrenica enclave in Tuzla was? Thank you. And I mean refugees from the municipalities that we can see on the screen before us. If you can recall the total number.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall the total number as I sit here without reference to a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we go back now to D16 -- D10 -- D106.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And before we have this before us on the screen, I'd like to ask you this: We've seen a number of reports that talk about the accommodation of refugees from Srebrenica and we also saw a summary review coming from the BH Army on the total number, the overall number, of refugees over those three days. Can you tell us, please, was it the case that on the first three days there was a large influx of refugees, whereas later on, around the 16th and 17th, there was another wave of refugees? Was that the case or not?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now if we can take a look at page 4 in Serbian and 65 ter 7205. Perhaps we can split the screen and put them side by side.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't recall at this time whether or not there was a second wave. I'd have to look at UN reports to that -- to know that. I can't, at this point -- I'm not saying there wasn't, but right now as we sit here 15 and a half years after the fact, I'm hazy on whether or not there was a second influx. But it's possible there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Joseph. But this is very important and relevant for the Trial Chamber because we see the number of people who were evacuated via the territory of Republika Srpska as opposed to the number who had arrived through the corridor, but we don't see that in your report.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now just please see page 4 of this document. And the Trial Chamber will easily see the discrepancy between the numbers that are given there in respect of the evacuation that the UNPROFOR was conducting of civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you just referred to difficulties with numbers. Page 20, line 19, you are recorded to having said: "Can we go back now to ... D106." I think that was D176; is that correct? Mr. Gajic nods and is in agreement with this statement.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But you assigned a new number. The Registrar said D0106, and that used to be 1D28. Or maybe I wrote it down incorrectly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I was told by the Registrar that it should be 1D -- sorry, I do make the same mistake. D176. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now take a look at 1D76, page 4, where we can find the table that was already shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Do you really mean 1D76 or D176?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Your microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'm referring to D176. And now we can see it on the right-hand side of the screen. We don't have it in Serbian but we are talking about numbers here, so this will do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So if you take a look at the numbers here, we can see that the BiH Army gives the correct number of people registered by them. They say in total of 29.336 people, and then they give the division according to localities. A moment ago we looked at another document where we saw that the numbers were smaller. So my question is as follows: If the BiH Army registered 29.336 persons during the first three days, on the 12th and on the 13th of July people who were coming through the territory of Republika Srpska then did the UNPROFOR register a higher or a lower number?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I would have to refer to documents and to see what really was the total number of persons registered. You say by UNPROFOR. UNHCR would have had the chief responsibility to do an accounting of the numbers. It's possible that UNPROFOR, because they were involved in the movement of these people, had data. But UNHCR would have had the primary responsibility to do a tabulation. And you volunteered the comment about the relevance of these numbers. I'm merely the witness here, but I would have thought the major relevance would be on the number of persons executed, not the number of persons evacuated. But I'm merely here as a witness and will continue to respond to your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Joseph. I'm not imputing anything to you. I'm not putting any pressure on your memory. I myself cannot remember some things so many years afterwards. I want to know one thing: Who registered the people coming out of the Srebrenica enclave and were there any lists made? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand the question, and that is quite a good question. And the answer is, I don't really know precisely who registered or if anyone did. Remember, it was quite a chaotic situation. And as I testified before, seeing these allegations that we were getting from women who were very agitated because their daughter or sister had gone missing or -- and some were allegedly raped, and so forth, when I heard these allegations from these women and saw the difficulty that UNHCR had to establish that, this was my lesson number one that I took with me when I was in Zepa. And when Viktor and I were there, we were determined, as best the two of us could, to keep a list. And even in that heat, with the pressure and the pace and the stress that we were under, we tried our best to do a list of every person on that bus in Zepa, to know that -- and to give that list later to UNHCR to know that every person would be accounted for and that, indeed, they would safely arrive. So I -- this is a valid point and a valid question about the persons from Srebrenica. And as I recall, it was problematic to know whether there were lists and who was keeping them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, since they have very precise figures here, I would like you to tell me the following: Did somebody make a log? We are not seeing rounded numbers here. It suggests that somebody was making lists and logs and then also ordering the necessary supplies, hygiene supplies, food packets, and so on.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to look back over the report that you saw that I drafted. And as you pointed out, some of that information, you could see that there was an effort on my part to try to get a handle on some statistics. And there was -- as it was reported, the source was the police there. But I -- I'm not sure here, speaking at this time, who was making or keeping a list. What I recall was at the time, and this is to, you know, give some context for -- about UNHCR, is we were overwhelmed. Our -- the major, again, preoccupation at that point in Srebrenica was taking care of these people, no matter how many, whatever number they were. And that was our -- and that was an overwhelming task, believe me, when you have an influx like that in a matter of hours, literally, and when you're not prepared for that influx. And so that was -- it was a logistical and operational effort, and I'm simply not sure at this time who did or did not keep good data. And I would suppose UNHCR would have a good answer on that. I recall that Madam Ogata, for example, came as the crisis continued, I think, maybe, I don't know, five or six days later. She came, herself, for a visit. So UNHCR was quite seized of the issue. But I can't give you a specific answer as to who was maintaining a precise log.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Joseph. You have given us very useful information to both sides in these proceedings. Since we are interested in the number of refugees and the number of survivors and so on, we are certainly going to find a way to determine those numbers. We are not going to tire you, our witness, with these things anymore. However, let us turn the next page of this document so that you can see what were the reasons for my questions. I want to figure out how many people were transferred on the 16th.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have page 5 of this document. This is D176. We have it on the screens now. Actually, we don't have it on the screens. Can we have D176, page 5. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So this is the chronology of events. We already looked at this. And I want us to move to page 5, the 16th of July, since you don't remember those logs and other things.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have page 5 of the chronology drafted by the BiH Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now, if you take a look at the fourth paragraph from the bottom, where it says, At 4.30 on the 16th of July ... Did you find it in English?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We just need to go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The following page in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the third paragraph from the top. We can see it now on the screen. Thank you to Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And it says here: "At 430 hours on the 16th of July," so we are talking about early morning, "the units of the 24th Division KoV," that was the Tuzla division, "and the above-mentioned units from other 2nd Corps divisions started an offensive in the general sector of Baljkovica." So we are talking about the forces from the 2nd Corps. "And the 2-kilometre-long enemy line was broken in the general Baljkovica sector in the morning, and a corridor was created in the area west of Tijanici village, Bojici village, Velika Kosa, and east of Poljane, elevation 290, Govedarica. Both flanks, sides of the corridor, are well secured. And unobstructed passage of troops and civilians is enabled towards Baljkovica, Nezuk, Medjedja, and Jajici. The above-mentioned enemy line was broken by the units of the 211th Liberation Brigade, the 242nd MZlbr, and the 243rd MPrb ..." and so on. "The first group went through at about 1300 hours," they are talking about the 16th, "and people continued going through the in the afternoon. And during the night, on the 16th and 17th July, 1995" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I have to interrupt you. You are reading so fast that the transcript is not following and the interpreters have many problems. Please slow down while reading.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I apologise to interpreters and the makers of the transcript. So I'll repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: "The first group went through at about 1300 hours, and people continued going through in the afternoon and during the night on the 16th of July, 1995, as well as during the day of the 17th of July, 1995. An occasional small group is still passing through." And then he gives the numbers for the 19th and the 20th of July and so on. And then the last paragraph on my page says: "According to rough estimate in our intelligence" --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page in Serbian, thank you. Now we can't see several words in the document, but he is giving the total estimate here. So actually we would need to have the original in order to see the numbers. I don't want to speculate about the numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, the English translation doesn't have an entry about numbers at this point. Is it said "text missing" two times. Therefore, I think there is no better original.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, I was quoting the meaning of the sentence. It was the last sentence on my page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Which goes: "According to a rough estimate in our intelligence, a total number of ... and then text is missing. So what they probably wanted to say is that up to that point such and such number had passed through. So my question is as follows: Mr. Joseph, do you know that on the 16th and the 17th, during the breakthrough, a certain number of persons managed to reach the Tuzla territory, the territory controlled by the Tuzla corps? Thank you. Or rather, they haven't arrived there but they managed to use the corridor made by the 2nd Corps forces and they managed to reach the zone of the 2nd Corps. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're asking me was I aware at the time about any of this, I'd have to refer to reports that I -- that you had earlier, the report that I drafted, and any other reports that I might have drafted or might have seen, to know what I knew at the time. The answer today is: I don't recall being aware of this. But if I referred to this somehow in a report or something like that, then obviously I was aware and might have been aware at the time. So I'd have to look at reports that I drafted. But answering now, I'm not able to shed light on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Joseph. Since you remember the reports, can you tell us the following: Does that mean that even in your reports there should be a difference between the numbers wrote in earlier and one or two days later? If everybody was entered into those numbers, both the people arriving through the territory opened by the BiH Army and the others. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm somewhat confused by the question and so I'm not sure I'm going to be able to answer it precisely. I'm not aware now of the significance of discrepancies that seem to be referred to here in numbers. You can see from my own reports that there was an effort on my part and my colleagues' part at the time to come up with some, as best we could, with -- to come up with some numbers, to know about the scale of the problem. But I'm not able to shed light on any discrepancies. And further, if I could add, I'm not really seeing the great relevance of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Joseph. Maybe you can't see it here but for both sides in the proceedings here it is very important to figure out those things. My question is: Do you allow for the possibility that the BiH Army did not give you any information on people who reached the 2nd Corps zone in Tuzla through the breakthrough using fighting? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just -- I don't really want to comment on that. I don't want to allow for that be possibility, and I don't want to disallow that possibility. I'm just not really a witness who's able to speak to what information may or may not have been transmitted by the 2nd Corps. I would not have been a primary contact for the 2nd Corps for such information. So I'm simply not able to speak to that issue with respect to the larger question of how many people were in -- arrived in Tuzla and how many people were back in Srebrenica in deep peril. Probably there are other ways to address that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Joseph. Can you now take a look at the third paragraph from the bottom in English, and in Serbian it's the first paragraph from the top, which goes on as follows: "In combat operations with the 28th Division and the 24th Division, the aggressor suffered significant losses. 20 bodies of enemy soldiers stayed behind in our territory. And according to the enemy reports that were intercepted by the PEB, they took 30 bodies back to the Zvornik hospital. Six enemy soldiers were captured alive and a self-propelled gun and a tank, which were immediately engaged in combat against the aggressor. Another self-propelled gun and an ammunition depot were set on fire in the Baljkovici village." My question is: During that period, did anybody report to you the number of those soldiers who were captured? Were they registered by the ICRC? And also, did anybody report the people who were killed in order for their bodies to be exchanged? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer to the first question is: I personally at this time don't recall anyone reporting the number of soldiers captured and nor do I think that that's something, again in the midst of dealing with the crisis of an influx of displaced persons, that we who were on the ground dealing with those persons pushed out of their homes in Srebrenica, dealing with them, those thousands there, whether this information -- we would probably not be primary recipients of that information. With respect to the second question, were they registered by the ICRC, I'm not now nor was I then a member of ICRC. And you know they're very discreet about their work and about their information, and so you'd have to consult ICRC about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now go to the next page in English. We can remain on the same page in Serbian. And I'm going to read out the fourth paragraph from the top in Serbian. Let's see which paragraph this is in English. The first one that we can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You say that these things did not interest the UNPROFOR, however, they say here the 18th of July --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I think this is the wrong statement. The witness explained the priority and the duty to register and to help the refugees. He didn't say that UNPROFOR was not interested in that. Continue, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I accept your comment. I was imprecise.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So here I want to quote the contents of this document, beginning with the date. "18th of July, 1995, UNPROFOR used their own vehicles to transport from Bratunac to Tuzla 86 wounded persons from the Srebrenica enclave." Thank you. My question is as follows. Since we are talking here about the wounded people, killed people, and ill people, that is the reason that I asked you whether somebody registered them with the UNPROFOR or ICRC, and you say they weren't registered. However, we see here that the UNPROFOR transported those people with their own transport. Thank you. So I'm not going to discuss this document with you anymore.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have now D155.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, again you just said: "You say they weren't registered." I never heard a comment like that from this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And again, Mr. President, I think we've seen some unnecessary confusion earlier. When General Tolimir jumps from topic to topic and area to area without saying so, it introduces another level of confusion. As we can see here, we're talking about people coming from Bratunac; we're not talking about people at the Tuzla airport, which is what the majority of the questions have been focused on. And it just doesn't help when we go to another section and General Tolimir makes conclusions based on his prior examination on another topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you used the document 65 ter 7205. That was a report drafted by Mr. Joseph. Are you tendering it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Yes, I wish to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: If I'm correct, there is a B/C/S translation to that document. Am I correct? This is a question for Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, we're pending translation on this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. In that case, as you used this document, there's no objection to add this document to the 65 ter exhibit list. Leave is granted to add it. And the document will be received as a Defence document, pending -- marked for identification pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document under 65 ter number 07205, Your Honours, would be assigned D00177.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Marked for identification pending translation. Before you continue with the document on the screen, we must have our first break now. We will resume quarter past 4.00. And I would like to give you guidance, Mr. Tolimir, as always, you have limited time for cross-examination; you should focus on those areas the witness can provide you with his personal knowledge. We adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We have on our screens the document we called up before the break. Can we have page 4 shown in e-court, please. Rather than reading out the entire document, we'll just look at a summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Look at paragraph 3. The document was signed. Page -- or, rather, the number is 3 in Serbian, the last paragraph, as well as in English. So there we have it. The third and last paragraph. "The units of the 28th" -- It's Rasim Delic writing this to Alija Izetbegovic as part of his report. He says: "The units of the 28th Division of the ground forces have fought their way out of Srebrenica. The units of the 28th Division have remained compact. They have had a string of successes in the temporarily-occupied territory and have inflicted major losses on the aggressor. So far they have six captured Chetniks alive. The units of the 28th Division, which is Srebrenica, linked up with the infiltrated units of the 2nd Corps. Through joint effort, they are continuing their combat in the temporarily-occupied territory and are soon expected to fully link up. Activities are underway to take advantage of the success achieved by the units in the breakthrough." This is my question: Since this is a report send by Rasim Delic to Alija Izetbegovic and it was sent on the 16th and he refers to a breakthrough and a number of captures individuals, did any of the representatives dealing with civilian affairs, those that you represented in Tuzla, did any of them investigate into these captured Serbs referred to by Rasim Delic? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you for that question. And I want to refer to the learned intervention of the President of the Chamber prior to this, which I appreciated very much, because I want to emphasise here for the Chamber, and recalling that these are -- these proceedings are made public, and I want to underscore that there was every bit equal interest on the part of UNPROFOR with respect to civilians and military of all three sides, be they Bosniak or Bosnian slash whatever term or Croat or be they Serb. So I want to -- that to be very, very clear, that there was, of course, keen interest in the welfare of Serbs, be they civilians or military who were captured, on the part of the UN. That being said, different agencies had different roles. And as you know, General Tolimir, ICRC had the lead with respect to prisoners of war, and so that would have influenced what kind of information that we would have. And you know very well ICRC is very discreet about who they share and release that information to. So it's possible, I cannot answer categorically who within UNPROFOR had information about these captured Serbs, but I can assure you, General Tolimir, that their welfare would have been a keen concern of ours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I asked you about this, and this is my next question: Unless prisoners of war are reported initially, isn't there a danger that they might just be reported as dead in combat? For instance, these captured soldiers here, unless registered with the international organisations, they could be later on reported, as in this case by the Muslims, as simply having died in combat? For instance, there's a reference in this document to 20 bodies. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is among the reasons why it is important to have a proper registration. And, as I said, that's a role that ICRC had the lead on, and I'm sure UNPROFOR military assets, if they were aware of this, would have been in contact with ICRC about that, as I was in contact with ICRC when it came to the disappearance of Colonel Palic, who was ultimately found executed not far from Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll get to that as well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have D55 shown. It's a report by Viktor Bezruchenko entitled, "The Fall of Zepa." We're interested in page 3. Let me state for the record that Bezruchenko was in Zepa with the witness. This should also provide an answer to Judge Mindua's question. Let us look at paragraph 8 of the report. There it is. We have it in English, it's page 3. It's page -- it's paragraph 2 in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: "The Zepa enclave was defended by the 285th Brigade of the BH Army under the command of Colonel Avdo Palic and it reported to the 28th Division in Srebrenica under Naser Oric's command. Naser Oric visited Zepa at least once in March of 1995." And there is a document referenced in the footnote to that effect. "According to a BH Army report, the strength of the 285th Brigade was at 100 per cent on the 13th of December, 1994." And so on and so forth. Let's look at line 8, where it reads: "As of the 7th of February," that's just after footnote 9. "As of 7 February 1995, the strength of the 285th Brigade was 1.122 officers and men." In footnote 10 there is a reference to the underlying document, and so on. Let's look at the penultimate line in paragraph 8, which reads: "The command of 285th Brigade was planning to, in case of such an eventuality," and this is a reference to the VRS, "request unspecified assistance from the 8th Operational Group to disarm the Ukrainian UNPROFOR company and take their personnel hostage." And now I'm reading the text in small print. This is Bezruchenko reporting: "By maximum use of configuration of the grounds, creating obstacles by expedient means of the main communications, suitable for armour and mechanised units of the enemy, as well as by engaging our main forces in these directions, to prevent enemy's entry into the depth of free territory. Besides that, by committing small diversionary groups in the depth of the enemy territory, to continuously de-concentrate enemy units. In critical moments, request co-operation -- co-ordinated action from elements of the unit of the 8th Operational Group," which is the one in Srebrenica. "Keep some elements of the unit on standby to take weapons away from the Ukrainian company and prevent them from leaving Zepa." So you can also see the original of the document. This is my question: Does it not transpire from this that the enclave was continuously used for sabotage actions directed at the territory of Republika Srpska, and was this not something that you and Bezruchenko were both aware of as a situation leading to an escalation of the conflict? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before I can answer, I need to clarify that this is the report of Viktor Bezruchenko, and if that's correct, I'd like to know the date that this report was written.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. The Defence is not aware of the date of this report since it was produced at the request of the Prosecution. It was produced by Mr. Bezruchenko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I can help you. It is in your list of documents and there it is written 22nd of June, 2010. This report was produced by Viktor Bezruchenko. But I would like to know, there is a paragraph which is a quotation from another document with a reference in footnote 12. Can we see, please, footnote 12. Yeah, this is in a document with a certain ERN number of the 13th December of 1994. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, as an Officer of the Court, I can provide a little bit of background to this military narrative that General Tolimir has made use of. Mr. Bezruchenko was an employee of the OTP for some time as a military analyst, I believe, was his formal title. He asked if he could prepare a report on the fall of Zepa, and that report was produced, I believe, sometime in late 2006 in at least a draft form to the Prosecution. It was provided unfortunately too late for any meaningful use in the prior trial and it's never been used as an exhibit by the Prosecution nor has Mr. Bezruchenko been called as a witness by the Prosecution, owing to its relative late date in the prior case. I believe that that 2010 date to which you referred, Mr. President, may have been some kind of disclosure date, but I believe it went over in May of 2008 in one form to the accused. So I'm not sure where that 2010 date came from, but I can tell you I personally saw a draft of this for the first time in 2006, to just give you a general date, so it's not contemporaneous certainly with the events. And as you can see, he was relying on documents, as Your Honour has noted, that he obtained in the course of his work as a military analyst. I'm being corrected by Ms. Stewart. This report was disclosed on 5 November 2009 to the Defence in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this information. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we'd like to thank the Prosecution for the additional information related to Mr. Viktor Bezruchenko's reports. Unfortunately, we weren't privy to all the information mentioned by the Prosecutor at this time. We didn't know that Mr. Bezruchenko was on an OTP team or, rather, that he was their military analyst. We weren't aware of that either. As far as the date of 2010 is concerned, we referred to the information contained in the tables produced to us by the OTP. So I'd have to check with my assistant to see why precisely that date was mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Nevertheless, we have now enough information about the background of this report. The question of Mr. Tolimir was: "Does it not transpire from this that the enclave was continuously used for sabotage actions directed at the territory of Republika Srpska, and was this not something that you and Bezruchenko were both aware of as a situation leading to an escalation of the conflict." This was the question. Sir, are you able to answer with this additional background information about the document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President, and thank you for reviewing the question. I was about to ask for that, so you read my mind. What I can answer, because I want to be very precise to be responsive. If the question is directed at the knowledge that Mr. Bezruchenko and I had at the time in 1995 specifically with respect to Zepa, I can only restate what I said at the beginning of my testimony this afternoon. We were generally aware that there were weapons. And here we see that a number of years after the fact, I guess maybe, let's see, 2009, 14 years or so, 12 to 14 years after the fact Viktor prepared a report, and we can see evidence of some very serious research on his part where he's come up with figures. But I emphasise: Well after the fact. Well after Viktor and I were on the road to Zepa in 1995. And so our awareness at that time -- perhaps Viktor had some other information, but I doubt it and -- because we were consulting with each other at the time, but we were aware, as I said, that there were weapons there. David Harland and I had proposed a demilitarisation plan. We wouldn't have done that if we didn't believe that there were weapons. We didn't have this number of precision. And as you see there, the bulk of them are small arms, not -- and just a couple of mortar pieces, not any heavy artillery, unlike their adversary. And -- but with respect to their military activities and the use of -- as the way General Tolimir has characterised it, as constantly used, or something like that, for sabotage actions, we, I think, again, were generally aware, as I said, that safe areas could be used and had been used. And I gave a personal example. But he and I -- I can't speak a hundred per cent for Viktor, but I don't recall any conversation. Speaking for myself, I did not have specific information as to what Colonel Palic and his troops were doing and the nature of the operations at that time, and, further, whether or not their operations were conducted against military targets or were they conducted against civilians as well, which might be interesting to know. And so we just simply did not have very specific information on that, and, again, our focus was elsewhere. Our focus was on this humanitarian operation which would ensue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I note that it is not the first time that the witness provided you with this answer. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Can the witness please say so when he thinks that I'm saying something that isn't right or that I'm not right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So this perception of operational activity as described in Mr. Bezruchenko's book, how can -- what sort of a reflection would that have on the civilian population, what sort of a bearing would that have on the civilian population living in the enclave of Zepa at that time? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I formed the impression that you are asking the witness for speculation. He provided you with his knowledge. And he didn't know about these facts at the relevant time. And now you are asking him to comment which bearing that would have for the civilian population. I don't see the purpose of such a question. Please move on to factual questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. It isn't for me to understand this. What matters is that you have an understanding. The witness said that it would be interesting to see what -- how things stood, so can we now have 1D568 which is an intelligence report from the Main Staff dated April of 1995 signed by myself. Can we have page 3 after we've seen page 1. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You can see that it says, "Main Staff of Republika Srpska, Intelligence and Security Sector."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have page 3, paragraph 4, the one that was indicated by the cursor a moment ago. I'll be reading it because it doesn't have a translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'm quoting: "It has been confirmed that the Muslim forces in Srebrenica, Zepa, and Gorazde are continuing with their preparations for offensive activities and that they have been using the Srebrenica-Zepa axis for their movement of forces, movement of civilians, and goods. They are using it as -- or, rather, the supplies of ammunition and weapon have been arriving by air. The majority of the population have expressed fear and wish to leave the enclave because of the announced escalation of combat activities and because of their feeling of isolation." Thank you. I've told the witness what it was that the Main Staff saw as happening as early as April of 1995, and this is my question: The combat activities carried out, out of the enclaves of Srebrenica and Zepa, did they have a bearing on the inclination of the population to leave the areas, and did they in any way induce this desire on their part? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see the -- I see the question now from the accused, and I would say that it is calling for some speculation and my part. Is it possible that combat actions taken by the Armija which would produce a reprisals from the Serb army would create anxiety among that population? Yes, that is -- that is quite possible. Can I then or now determine that that was the precipitating cause or how much that was present in the minds of the population? I don't know. But, General, I think we should both be clear in our understanding that the anxiety would be with respect to the reprisal actions by Serb forces and that that would be the source of the anxiety on the part of the population. Whether it was preceded by an attack by the Armija or, as you might well know in some other instances or perhaps in this instance, whether it was not preceded by such a case, we don't know. But ultimately, their fear would be actions taken by your side.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I asked you this because of the status of the zone, because Zepa had the status of a demilitarised zone, which status was not achieved by combat but through peace negotiations. That's why I'm asking you this. Was this considered by the UNPROFOR command in Sarajevo, that this sort of activities should not be allowed to be taking place out of the enclaves in order for them not to be deprived of their status? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that in general, yes, that is correct. The fact that safe areas were not completely demilitarised was a concern in general in UNPROFOR. And I'm going to restate that the reason why they were not fully demilitarised is an equally valid one that deserves some discussion and inquiry, and I'm hopeful that perhaps General Smith or others could shed some light on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since we don't have any time left, can we have another look at D55, Mr. Bezruchenko's report entitled, "The Fall of Zepa."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before we leave this document, I would like to see the first page again, to see a date on that. It's not very legible. It could be April 1995. On top we see a handwritten date, 23rd of April, 1995. Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir, are you tendering this document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Yes, I would like to tender it, if you are willing to admit it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be marked for identification pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The three-page document under 1D00568, Your Honours, will be assigned D00178 marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now have D55 once again. That's Mr. Viktor Bezruchenko's report entitled, "The Fall of Zepa." And specific page 18, paragraph 65. Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We can see paragraph 65 before us now. That's the second paragraph in English and the fourth paragraph in the Serb version. And I will read from the fourth line in paragraph 65, where it says: "The BH strategy was to -- the BH strategy was to deny presence of BiH Army units in Zepa, Srebrenica, and Gorazde, to attribute military operations to unarmed people, and not to acknowledge any discussions on evacuation. The chief of department, Fikret Muslimovic, sent his suggestions for interviews with foreign journalists to Zepa leadership." And then Mr. Bezruchenko mentions those three suggestions by the chief of department of the BH Army. The first: "Never mention military units in Zepa, Srebrenica, and Gorazde." Two: "What the army is doing in this area, say that it is being done by the people." Three: "No mention of evacuation should ever be made." And Mr. Bezruchenko actually took this from a document which was marked as 101 with a -- he mentions a document in footnote 101. My question for you would be: Before you arrived in Zepa, were you briefed on the fact that the BH Army on the 16th of July, 1995, had attacked UNPROFOR -- my apologies, my question is wrong. That will be my next question. I've skipped one. So my question is this: Can these and similar psychological and propaganda activities, in terms of not negotiating with the BH Army on the Zepa issue in view of the fact that they deny that there were any military units there -- so did the UNPROFOR know or was it indicated to the UNPROFOR by the BH leadership that there were no armed units in Zepa, no BH Army armed units? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know exactly what representations were made by the BH leadership that you are referring to there, to UNPROFOR. I've already stated that it was understood in UNPROFOR that there were arms there. And I told you David Harland and I even proposed our own demilitarisation. So -- but with respect to what was actually communicated by the BH leadership, I don't have the answer to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, that's precisely why I put this question as an introduction to the topic of demilitarisation. But of course that's difficult if the Muslims are denying -- or were denying that there were any armed units within the enclaves. Now I will put the question that I mentioned a little earlier. Before you arrived in Zepa, you and Mr. Bezruchenko, were you briefed that immediately preceding your arrival there on the 16th of July, 1995, the BH Army in Zepa had attacked UNPROFOR and seized a sizeable quantity of weapons from UNPROFOR? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me first respond to your comment about my response. This document -- this report of Viktor Bezruchenko in paragraph 65 is referring to media strategy, that putative media strategy on the part of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina personnel, and you're conflating that with what we knew. We were not media. We were not journalists. We were UNPROFOR. We had UNPROFOR assets, as your subsequent question refers to, on the ground. So it's not terribly central for the information of UNPROFOR -- we're not depending on journalists to know what we know or depending on a certain media message or spin, when we have an UNPROFOR unit in the form of the Ukrainians that's on the ground, and presumably quite aware of the fact that there are weaponry there, and presumably quite aware that there are formed units there, and presumably sharing this information with UNPROFOR there. So I'm not necessarily seeing the connection of those two. And with respect to this point about threats and attack on UNPROFOR, we were aware of reports from the Ukrainians, yes, of threats and presumed shooting incidents. And I think, as I mentioned before, it's important to have sympathy for the position of the Ukrainians being in the midst of a bombardment and these kinds of shooting incidents and threats, et cetera. So, yes, we were aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I will refrain from commenting on this, but I'll revisit this question. Now, let's take a look at paragraph 54 of Mr. Bezruchenko's report because you've just said that you did know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
