utterances.text: [Interpretation] And can we now please see the next page, page 20 of this report, where paragraph 74 is. Page 20, paragraph 74. Thank you. We have 15 before us. Can we now have 20. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now, if we look at paragraph 74, it reads as follows - thank you: "BiH attack against UNPROFOR did not go unnoticed by VRS. On 16 July, Tolimir reported that the Muslim forces attacked and overran UNPROFOR OP7, Donji Slap, Observation Post 8, stop, OP1, Brezova Rava, and OP9, Pripecak. In these attacks, UNPROFOR reportedly lost 4 APCs, three 14.5 millimetre heavy machine-guns, three 7.62 millimetre PKT machine-guns, 15 automatic assault rifles, four generators, three radio sets, and 15 bulletproof vests." And Mr. Bezruchenko mentions a document in footnote 112 to corroborate this. Now my question for you is this: Before you left for Zepa, did you have occasion to read this report about the assets that were seized by the Muslims from UNPROFOR? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that we did. I would only hasten to add that Viktor Bezruchenko is Ukrainian and was a former Ukrainian officer and had good means of communications. Its quite possible that Viktor was aware of this. Maybe he shared this information with me. Possibly we knew. But at this time I can't remember whether or not we had this specific information at that time, as the two of us went to Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, this was a large quantity of weapons.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, can we see document D015, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And while we are waiting for it to come up, let me just say that it's a report by Avdo Palic entitled, "Planning." And in the relevant portion that I would like to refer you to, it says, and I quote: "The UNPROFOR was disarmed according to instructions issued earlier." Let's take a look at the document, I don't want to read any further.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's D105. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please take a look at this. And the mid part of the document signed by Avdo Palic on the 16th of July, it says, and I quote: "We are disarming UNPROFOR in accordance with the directive we received earlier." My question is the following: What was the situation within the Ukrainian Battalion that you could observe when you arrived there with Mr. Bezruchenko? And had UNPROFOR been disarmed as it is stated in this report here?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am going to do my best to recall here and access whatever visual memory from 15 and a half years ago. When we got there, I recall the Ukrainian soldiers as being in a relatively normal state such as that situation was. They weren't in a state of hyper-anxiety that I can recall. And I believe - I'm hazy here and cannot be a hundred per cent sure - but I believe that they still had some weapons. I think that they still had Kalashnikovs and so forth. So I can't speak to the -- whether or not they were 100 per cent disarmed or how much of their equipment had been taken by Armija and so forth. Essentially they were very aware and we were aware that the situation of that enclave had changed dramatically, and all of us, the Ukrainians and ourselves, at that point were not focused on recovering their kit or such things. We were all focused on a situation that was in crisis with the two sides here, their forces very close with Serb armament right there and which had been used and with Armija forces up in the hills, and that's the situation. That's what we -- and they very quickly, the Ukrainians, especially having Viktor there, proceeded to work closely with us and to try to be helpful in support of this, the movement of the population, which is what we asked them to do.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to tender -- oh, my apologies. It's already been admitted. Can we now see document 1D598, please. 1D598. Thank you. I have to note that I've asked for a document where Akashi is the author, and the document is -- this communication was sent to Annan, Mr. Annan. And if we could have page 2 of this document in e-court. There seems to be a problem. Thank you. Now I have it before me. Could we now see page 2 of this document that was sent by Mr. Akashi to Mr. Annan on the 11th of July, 1995. If we can have the next page of that document, please, and then the second paragraph. Thank you. We have the second paragraph. And in English that will be the third paragraph on the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It says: "At 1220 hours today, I authorised a request for close air support against any Serb targets that may attack the Netherlands' blocking position south of Srebrenica as well as any heavy weapons identified to be shelling UN positions in the village of Srebrenica, or attacking observation posts along the perimeter of the enclave." My question: Did UNPROFOR have different standards in terms of air support? Because we see in this document that the Serbian army is threatened by possible air-strikes by NATO, whereas no action is taken on the other side, although three APCs had been seized, and that's heavy weaponry. So my question is: Was the UNPROFOR -- did the UNPROFOR actually have double standards in this situation? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Tolimir, you know I'm not going to characterise -- provide a response that characterises this in the way that you are asking, because, as you well know, addressing this question requires a great deal of context, including the very important point that when NATO air-strikes had been conducted earlier that year in response to the mortar attack from your forces in Tuzla that killed on the order of 70, possibly more - I'm going by memory - Muslims in Tuzla, most of them young people, and a greet deal of them completely non-combatants, including, I'm sure, quite a number of female, and responding to that, UNPROFOR called on NATO air-strikes which resulted in your forces taking UN hostages. So that's an important contextual point here. And so far you've not shown me any documents that show that in Zepa Ukrainian forces were taken hostage. You have not shown me anything about that. And we -- as -- you mentioned there were threats and possibly more, but we -- we don't see hostages taken, which one would presume would be one of the easiest steps that could have been taken in that situation, and we don't see that. So we have to -- these things, as I have suggested to you, require a great deal of context to understand. And we also know, contextually, that following -- since you introduced this point about Srebrenica, that following that one very limited air-strike there, we know that it was not followed by other air-strikes, and we know, eventually, that Srebrenica capitulated and that Muslim civilians, Muslim men, who sought shelter in UNPROFOR-controlled areas, we know were given to your forces, and we know that the vast majorities of those men perished, executed by your forces. So that's all contextual -- important contextual aspects of this to note and to answer with respect to questions of double standards. And if you want to get into particulars about decision-making on this, again, General Smith would be a very good witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You told the Trial Chamber about what you knew. Now, could you tell us, if you know, when this event occurred in Tuzla? Was that in August? And then perhaps you can tell us the time of the crisis with UNPROFOR in Sarajevo. So were those two events separated by several months? Would you know?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believe -- I'm going by memory here, but I believe that Tuzla mortar attack or artillery was in the spring -- was in April, possibly. April or May of that year. But that we know, regardless of the time-frame, this was the same year, and that result of hostage taking was quite significant event in how UNPROFOR and NATO approached the question of calling on NATO for air support.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. But I will repeat my question and please try and answer it. Were the events in Tuzla in April or were they in August? Can you just tell us what you can recall.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not in August. Going by memory, I think that they may well have been in April. But I can't confirm that, and I'm sure that it's quite easy enough for us to confirm that it was in April. It was not in August; it was in April. But those events heavily influenced the approach. Those were -- those were quite significant events. And when I bring them into context, it's not to be tendentious; it's because that was quite relevant context from the very same year.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We talked here about events that happened months between each other. Can you now tell us how they relate to each other. I'm asking you about the events in July 1995, the two enclaves, the attack on UNPROFOR forces, and a different response to that, whereas one side was receiving threats, on the other hand we have the situation where the public wasn't even informed of the infringement on the part of the other side. So was all of that, the escalation of forces in the enclaves arming and the conflict that ensued, were all those things mutually interlinked? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Tolimir, I don't want to get into a debate with you. I don't think it's my role here to debate with you. You're wanting me to engage in some kind of a commentary that either addresses or rebuts the allegation that there was a double standard. My prior answer, I thought, provided necessary context here, including the absence of hostage taking in Zepa. You raised Srebrenica. If you raise Srebrenica again, I will again raise the necessary context including the most important point which is what happened to the Muslim men there that were under control of your forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We are not adversaries here, so I won't comment any further on this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document, 1D598, and move on to a new topic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I think we are in a similar situation with the last report of Mr. Akashi to the Secretary-General Kofi Annan, and we marked that previous document for identification to use it with the Witness Rupert Smith. I have the impression that we are in a similar situation with this document. Would you agree to that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I agree with all your proposals. Yes, we should mark it as such because it speaks on the subject that it speaks on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And General Smith is mentioned as one of the recipients of this document. It will be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document number 1D00598 will be assigned D00179 marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Can we now have D55 in e-court. That is Bezruchenko's report entitled, "The Fall of Zepa." Page 23, please. Paragraphs 86, 87, and 88. Thank you. So can we have paragraph 86 to begin with.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So in paragraph 86, we can see the following: "At this point, UNPROFOR Sector Sarajevo began preparations for evacuation of civilians from Zepa. UNPROFOR operations order dated 20th of July made the following assessment of the situation: BiH Defence of Zepa has collapsed, and surrender of the enclave to BSA has been accepted. Large numbers of DPs wishing to seek refuge in federation-controlled territory will therefore have to be moved." And Mr. Bezruchenko, in the footnote 131, also gives the reference to the official document on the basis of which he wrote paragraph 86. And then paragraph 87 goes on as follows: "The order to determine the UNPROFOR mission as follows," so we are talking about that operative order dated the 20th of July. I quote: "In conjunction with BiH government and UNHCR, UNPROFOR is to co-ordinate the evacuation of DPs from Zepa to Zenica." And then Mr. Bezruchenko references the relevant document in the footnote 132. And then paragraph 88: "The evacuation operation was supposed to be executed in three stages and involve UNPROFOR forces of Sector Sarajevo, Sector North-East, Sector South-West, as well as HQ UNPROFOR, (rear)." The reference we find in footnote 133. My question is as follows --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could the document be scrolled to the bottom, please, to see the -- thank you very much. Was a little bit too far. We need both the paragraph and the footnote. Thank you. Now your question, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Your microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Joseph, as far as you know, when did UNPROFOR begin with the preparations for the evacuation of the population of Zepa? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will defer to the research of Mr. Bezruchenko in this report. It seems Viktor has done solid research on this. We know from the -- Mr. Harland's reports when Mr. Bezruchenko and I were dispatched two times, and so those would constitute preparations in some respect from our civil affairs sector, and I'm deferring here to this report with respect to other sectors. When I mean "sectors," not geographic, but what the UNPROFOR military was doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So can I then make the conclusion that it was the 20th, as Bezruchenko himself says in his report, because you basically deferred to him? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me be clear, I'm not in a position here to affirm every date and fact and assertion made by Mr. Bezruchenko in this report. I'm not able to do that, not because I don't want to do that, but because my memory of events 15 and a half years ago is limited. So it looks like Viktor has produced solid research here, but I'm not in a position to -- here for the Chamber to absolutely affirm the -- his -- the assertions that he makes, but I have no reason to doubt them either.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Joseph, for your answer. Now can you tell us the following: Did the attack of the 20th of July, the attack carried out by the BiH Army on the UNPROFOR in Zepa, represent a breach of the agreement that had been signed? And can you also tell me whether that marked the beginning of combat activities directed outside from the enclave, including the attack on the UNPROFOR? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will answer in the following way: Any attack on UNPROFOR at any time by any party in any location, whether a safe area or not, would be in violation of obligations on the part of the parties. So any attack by any party at any time, whether or not in a safe area. And the answer is, no, I am not in a position now to tell you whether that event marked the beginning of combat activities. And one should be careful about the term "combat activities." What does that mean? Those specific attacks related to that or other things including interruption of supplies? One would have to examine what the definition is of combat activities. And again I'd have to also look at records, and others would have to, about what was the nature of the fighting in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday we saw a video showing that Mr. Torlak attended a meeting with General Mladic on the 19th. And there he said, We all agree that we should leave the enclave. And then Mladic said, We are going to enable you to leave as you wish. My question is: If the Muslim army attacked the UNPROFOR a day later, on the 20th, and seized their heavy weaponry, as I read out a few moments ago, does that represent a violation of the agreement that Torlak had achieved with General Mladic? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, maybe I've lost it in the transcript, but I'm just wondering what that cite was for the proposition that there was a Muslim attack on the 20th that he -- is this a reference to the Bezruchenko report? And if so, which paragraph contains that? I've just simply lost the thread. If there's a particular paragraph where this attack on the 20th is referenced, if we could just have that back up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you help us, Mr. Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Can we now see page 25 in this report that is currently on the screen. I'm interested in paragraph 94. Now we can see it. Now, take a look at the third line in paragraph 94, beginning with the words: "In an attempt to seise UNPROFOR's weapons, on 20th of July ABiH attacked the compound of the UKRCOY with heavy machine-gun-fire and hand-grenades. The second floor of the UKRCOY building was hit with a heavy weapon which destroyed the first-aid station and medicine stock. As fighting for the enclave continued, UNPROFOR Sector Sarajevo described the situation in Zepa as of the 21st of July as critical." And then in the footnote 140 we have the reference for this. And now that we have reached this point, he goes on to say: "ABiH made threats to kill Ukrainian soldiers, while VRS continued shelling of ABiH positions." Footnote 141. "The ABiH 285th Brigade Commander Palic emphasised that a delegation of BHC forward, Ukrainian Battalion," and so on and so forth, "should get to Zepa." I think that we can now see based on this that that was on the 20th of July, 1995. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Yeah, I just wanted to make sure because we hadn't seen this paragraph before and that's why I was -- I thought I had lost the trail. My question is - and it's just for the sake of making sure we've got a clear understanding - is: Is the Defence's position that when they refer to a BiH attack that this was an unprovoked attack or a single start of an attack? I think that's an important issue to have resolved in the context of this question. I'm certainly prepared to deal with this on re-direct. There are lots of documents I can use with the witness. But it will help clarify, I think, now what the General's position is with respect to when he describes a BiH attack on the 20th of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, you may deal with that in re-examination. It was a long time ago that you put a question to the witness. You should repeat it, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did the disarming of UNPROFOR on the 20th of July, 1995 -- was it an event that you knew about? And did you and Bezruchenko inform the Sarajevo command about it? How could it affect the civilian population, bearing in mind that it wasn't the UNPROFOR who started attacking the population? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken, this is a different question than that you put to the witness earlier. But I will not interrupt. The witness should answer, if possible.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the specific question of did we know about this, these developments - and this quite serious -- and let me say that it's quite serious what's reported here in paragraph 94 - I cannot recall whether we knew this -- had this information or not. I can state that we would not -- based on our initial trip to Zepa, we were only at OP2, and we did not go and were not permitted to go down to the village, as I said, we were sent away. So we did not have firsthand reporting on this, but it's possible, when we returned to Sarajevo, that we were made aware of some of this. I don't recall the detail. And, again, when we returned to Zepa, these kinds of concerns were not on the minds of the Ukrainians that we -- this was not something that they were shouting to us about and pointing fingers. All of us were -- had a different focus. You referred earlier to the video. And, again, I would only -- and you said was this somehow in contravention of the agreement, and, again, I restate what I told you, that we were not there, in our view, at least, pursuant to that agreement. We were there understanding that there had been some sort of a capitulation in general and that evacuation was coming. And that was our purpose in being there, not in implementation of points in that agreement. I just mention that because that was once again mentioned, that agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Nyambe has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Actually just a clarification. Your answer right now answers the first part of the question that General Tolimir asked you. The second part was: How did it affect the civilian population, bearing in mind that it wasn't the UNPROFOR who started attacking the population. Could you try to answer that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, let me try to answer that. If I understand the question, it is that how did the firing by the Armija onto the Ukrainians affect the civilian population; is that the question I'm meant to answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: I think the question is how it could affect, not how it affected.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: How it could affect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It could be -- it could make the -- agitate the population. It would be one more example of how the security in that area had deteriorated. I'd have to look -- if we want to know about the mental state of the population, of course we would have to bear in mind when bombardment commenced, and I'd have to -- I've lost sight now of where we are in the sequence, but one can also imagine that the bombardment from the other side would have injected quite a bit of anxiety as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you, on the 16th during the first attack of the Muslims on UNPROFOR, as we have seen that Bezruchenko wrote in his document, and also during the attack on the 20th, did you see any shelling carried out by VRS towards the Muslims, or did you see any sort of activity of the VRS directed towards UNPROFOR or the Muslims, or did you receive any sort of report about it? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't speak to the developments of the 16th. And, again, I'm going to restate my reporting and restate, General, that I have no reason to dispute or challenge the record as its reported by Mr. Bezruchenko. So if he reports a certain attack on a certain date, I have no reason to dispute that. My contribution here -- or to affirm it. So I'd say again, my contribution here is to try and be a witness for things that I saw there in Zepa, and what we witnessed was -- the first date may have been the 19th of July, when we were there, meeting with General Mladic, and there were others there meeting too, was -- what we witnessed was and heard was the commencement of artillery that we were rather sure was from your side. And as we see from the report of Mr. Bezruchenko, the other side didn't have artillery. They had two mortars, if my memory recalls, from what I read here. So we presume that that artillery that we heard was from your side, and that would have been on the 19th. What happened on the 16th or other dates, again, I'm reading Viktor's report as you are reading it, and I have no basis to dispute what Viktor has in his report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could there have been any activity of the Muslims towards the UNPROFOR which could be justified by what the Muslims did -- by what the Serbs did to the Muslims? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, I think I testified earlier, not very long ago, that any attack by any party on UNPROFOR, including these attacks -- and I think I just said that, reading this report, this is quite graphic and very serious, these reports of attacks by Armija on UNPROFOR, and I think I stated very, very clearly that these are all unacceptable. Including these attacks. And not justifiable. And in violation of obligations. All of those things.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We don't have more time to go into a more detailed discussion about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. Tolimir, time is always limited. We are reaching the time for the second break. But I would like to ask you, have you any idea how much time you will need for completion of your cross-examination? For planning purposes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. It's hard to estimate right now, bearing in mind that we are spending lots of time to minor -- discussing minor issues and me getting irrelevant answers. I'm going to try to give you the estimate after the break. Probably I'm going to drop some of my questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, it's in your hands if you discuss minor issues or relevant issues. You should focus, indeed, on relevant issues. I hope, Mr. Thayer, there's no other witness waiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, because of the realities of time estimates, we have had a witness ready to go in case the cross-examination went short. Given the colloquy, we'll release the witness with the Trial Chamber's permission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That's fine. That was a very reasonable decision. We must have our second break now and resume quarter past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, just to inform everyone in the courtroom that the Defence will do its best to complete its cross-examination of this witness through the end of the day today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I just want to let the Trial Chamber and the Defence know, from our calculations, they've asked for 7 to 8 hours, I think they still have an hour left from that 8 hours, given the manner of some of the cross-examination, I'm going to require some time for re-examination. Right now I'd estimate about half on hour. So I think either way we're very likely to go into tomorrow, so I just didn't want to -- there to be any misunderstanding that it's got to be done today. Because I don't think it's going to happen today. And I just want to let the Defence know that from our perspective they've got an hour that they've asked for at least, so we're in no rush.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would agree. I wouldn't expect that we could finish today. Regrettably, Mr. Joseph, you will have to come back tomorrow, but it will be a quite short last session. Mr. Tolimir, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. If we all work together, we will do our best, as my Legal Advisor already mentioned, to make this -- to complete with this in due course. Can we now please see D56. This is a letter that the War Presidency and the Zepa command sent to President Alija Izetbegovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We see that the date on this letter is the 26th of July, 1995, and it was sent at 8.45 in the evening, sent to the president of the Presidency, Alija Izetbegovic, and it was signed by Zepa municipality representatives and the command of the 285th Brigade. And I will read from it: "President, minister, the negotiations at Boksanica attended by General Smith, the criminal Mladic, and Hamdija Torlak, the chairman of Zepa municipality, Executive Committee ended this evening. Nothing was agreed in these negotiations because General Smith did not bring the agreement on the all-for-all exchange, but today I was informed by the General Staff that the agreement on all-for-all exchange had been accepted by our side and that General Smith had taken it with him. General Smith stated in the presence of Hamdija Torlak that you were seeking a few more concessions for the exchange to take place." I won't read any further. My question is this: Did you attend this meeting attended by General Smith that Avdo Palic mentions in his letter to Alija Izetbegovic? And thank you. Please try to be quick and to the point. Just answer with a yes or no. And then when I put the next question, you can say what it was that you want. Were you present or not; yes or no? If you were, I will have an additional question; and if not, then I'll just skip it.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I might have attended. If this is the meeting I'm thinking, I believe I might have been present for this meeting in Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, please take a look at the last sentence of this letter. Actually, the last two sentences: "We repeat," Palic comments, "that General Smith stated that you did not agree to an all-for-all exchange and that you have not signed the agreement. Please reply regarding this matter as soon as possible." And then its signed with War Presidency and command of the 285th Light Brigade. Did General Smith tell Torlak that Alija Izetbegovic had not accepted the agreement on an all-for-all exchange?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't recall whether General Smith told him that or not. He might have or he might have just been stating to all concerned his understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you don't recall, can I refer you to this telegram that was sent by Palic to Mr. Izetbegovic, and I won't have any further questions regarding this. But could we now see D55, paragraph 109.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Stop for a moment, please. Stop for a moment. Mr. Tolimir, twice you said that this was signed by Avdo Palic. I don't he see the name Avdo Palic anywhere on this document. I don't see a signature. Can you help us with that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We see that its type-signed, Zepa municipality War Presidency. And if you recall, that is those three members of the War Presidency. And then it says the command of the 285th LB --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I understand this is your interpretation of this document. That might be right, but I'm just asking where you would see the name of Avdo Palic. I don't see it, and I wanted to put that on the record, because there's no signature and any indication that he himself signed it or a member of the War Presidency. I don't know that. We don't see it. That's all I want to --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. This is an e-mail telegram that was sent to Mr. Alija Izetbegovic. But you can interpret it in any way you wish. But I believe that Avdo Palic is the one who sent this. He was a member of the Presidency. And he addresses the president and the minister with, Mr. President and minister. And, of course, e-mail cannot be signed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: There's no need to repeat that. I just wanted to state for the record there's no name listed. Please continue with the next document that you asked for.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to tender this document into evidence. And also if we can pull up D55 now, paragraph 109.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I have a problem with this motion, with your tendering, because the witness couldn't say anything about the content. Mr. Smith might have conveyed this message or not. He was not sure if he attended this meeting. I would suggest you do the same and put it to General Smith when he will arrive and testify. First Mr. Gajic then Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I believe this has already been admitted, and its a document under D56. That's how it was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. That was the common understanding of both parties.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We see before us Bezruchenko's report, paragraph 109, where it reads as follows: "On the 26th of July, 1995, President Izetbegovic sent a message to Palic demanding to put under control the soldiers who were going to surrender. The message also contained a vague promise that an exchange would be arranged." And I'm now quoting from a portion that Mr. Bezruchenko singled out: "There is information that a certain number of your soldiers is moving towards the village with an intention to surrender. I don't know if it is correct. Warn them about the danger and put them under control. Negotiations about exchange are in progress. We have enough arguments to obtain good terms of exchange because we keep a great number of their prisoners, but we have to be careful about what we are doing," and so on and so forth, signed Alija Izetbegovic. Avdo Palic replied to this telegram, and I quote: "Mr. President, we received both your letters and the agreement that you sent. I ask you, and let this remain between you and me, are you ready to exchange us, the people from Zepa, a total of 2.500 people who have come from Srebrenica to Zepa, for all Chetniks?" My question is this: In your conversations with Avdo Palic or from them, were you able to conclude whether he wanted an evacuation both of military or able-bodied men and civilians from Zepa?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall the exact conversation on this issue, but my impression was that he was interested in an evacuation of both, that he was. That was my clear impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Very well. Now, tell us, please, based on the documents that Mr. Bezruchenko presented here, can it be inferred that Alija Izetbegovic prevented or wanted to pre-empt the arrival of soldiers to Zepa and their disarming?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Tolimir, let me answer that question this way. And this is very interesting to read Mr. Bezruchenko's report, and its an interesting question. You, before the break, suggested that -- put into the record a comment that I understood to be that my answers are less than relevance, that they're perhaps irrelevant at times, and I really am doing my best to be responsive here. This is quite interesting material that is presented here, and it would be equally interesting to see intercepts between Karadzic and his civilian and/or military leaders and for me to comment on those. And maybe he would things with respect to Serb intentions in Eastern Bosnia. And that would be interesting for me, to see and to comment on it, and I might be able to infer a conclusion about what Serb intentions were in Eastern Bosnia. I'm hear here as a fact witness. If you want me to change my role as a expert witness and give analysis and commentary, I can do that, but I've answered the question based on my knowledge as a fact witness. Avdo Palic seemed to me to be interested in this. What was going on in Sarajevo I had only limited information about. It may be as you suggest. It may be that President Izetbegovic was reluctant. Maybe it was for the reason that there was still, for him, the question of what happened to the men in Srebrenica. Or maybe it was some other interest. I don't know that. I don't know for sure. So I hope that answer is relevant. I'm certainly attempting to be relevant and responsive.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. What you have requested, to see, namely, the communications of the Serb side, that's something that the Prosecutor I'm sure can explore in his redirect.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I would request that we pull up document 65 ter 2438, page 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: While we are waiting for it to come up, that would be page 9 in Serbian and 8 in English, a question for Mr. Harland for the 26th of July, 1995. And he, here, gives his own assessment, and I'm referring to Mr. Harland, probably based on what he knew. And let me just read the last four lines of the last paragraph where it says "assessment." And then the fourth line from the bottom where it says: "Sarajevo, however, has no particular interest in letting the Serbs take Zepa without paying a price (a military price in terms of lost life, and a political price in terms of the fallout from the cleansing operation)." These are the words of Mr. Harland. Now, my question is this: Can you tell us whether he wrote this based on some information that he had either from Zepa or Sarajevo, and can you tell us what was the understanding of this at UNPROFOR, because that's implied here?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Let me answer in this way: First, let me state the obvious, that as with the report of Mr. Bezruchenko, this is the report of Mr. Harland. I'm not Mr. Harland, so I can't answer definitively about the basis for his assessment. That's number one. Number two, the point that you are getting at is focused on decision-making and tactics at the high level in Sarajevo, so it's unlikely that the basis for him to write this about exacting a price would have come from information based in Zepa. It would be logical that -- because it's referring to high-level decision-making, that that would be coming from -- the basis for that would be coming from Sarajevo. And what was the understanding of this at UNPROFOR, the other part of your question, the -- I think it's fairly clear, on its face, what the report is stating. The report is suggesting that there might be motives on the part of the Bosniak side at the high level that are influencing and complicating the negotiations on the prisoner exchange. And as we saw on the prior thing, the view from Zepa was of desperation with respect to their fate of what would happen to these guys who were on the ground, surrounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, please tell us, did you and Mr. Bezruchenko receive any information on where the Muslim army was going to go, bearing in mind that they did not want to sign the agreement and they did not want to hand over their weapons in accordance with the decision made by the War Presidency? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer to this question is, no, I do not recall us, that is, Mr. Bezruchenko or myself, receiving any information about where the Armija might be going, Muslim army as you call. No. We did not have that -- I don't recall information about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you in possession of any information about what happened later on to the able-bodied men from Zepa? I mean by this, did UNPROFOR have any such information? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not sure exactly what information UNPROFOR had at the time. As we all later learned, much later, the -- a great number of the Muslim men who were hiding there fled across the Drina River into Serbia and they were interned in camps in Serbia and survived until the end of the war, thus sparing them the fate of what happened to their brethren in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now let us take a look a D55, page 35, paragraph 123. Thank you to e-court. Okay. Now we are waiting to see it. And when with see it, we will see what the Muslim sources say. And then I will pose my question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So this is D55 again, Bezruchenko's report, where, on page 35, paragraph 123, he lists the sources, the BiH Army sources, which said what happened after Muslim soldiers refused to sign the agreement. I quote paragraph 123. You have it now on the screen. I quote: "According to BiH Army documents, on the 30th of July, VRS launched an attack from the direction of Bukovik, broke the Defences of the 285th Brigade, and seized dominant hill Zlovrh. Chief of Staff of the 385th Brigade Ramo Cardakovic ordered the elements of the Brigade to withdraw in the direction of Srebrenica to the area called Vukolin Stan. After all soldiers of the 285th Brigade assembled in the area, Ramo Cardakovic suggested that the Brigade should move in the direction of Poljanica, where it should cross the Drina and surrender to the Serbian forces. Up to 800 soldiers led by Ramo Cardakovic and assistant for security Salih Hasanovic crossed into Serbia and surrendered to SRJ authorities. The main body of the brigade split into several groups, and each was acting on its own, without centralised command. A group of about 200 men under Hurem Sahic succeeded to reach Kladanj across VRS-held territory on the 2nd of August. Another group of about 50 men, originally from Visegrad, under Samir Cocalic set off for Gorazde or Priboj in Serbia. Another group of up to 300 soldiers, originally from Srebrenica, who arrived to Zepa after Srebrenica collapsed went back to Srebrenica hoping to break through to Tuzla along the same route as used by the 28th Division. Yet another group about a company size under Sefik Zejnilovic went in the direction of Susica in the area of Crni Potok, where it intended to stay for a long time. This plan was based on the fact that there was a big cache of food hidden in the area. A small group of about seven men crossed the VRS-held territory and joined the BiH Army 243rd Motorised Brigade in the zone of responsibility of the 2nd Corps. Yet another small group of 14 soldiers reached Gorazde on the 3rd of August."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I would like to interrupt you at this point in time. This is a very time-consuming conduct of your cross-examination. You are reading a long part of a document written by another person, by Mr. Bezruchenko. You should put questions to this witness. He is now available for you for your cross-examination. Put questions, question after question. Not reading such a long text. He can't recall that and I can't recall that. Please continue and put questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Joseph, according to this report written by Bezruchenko and also based on the Muslim documents, it is possible to say that the whole brigade was evacuated to the territories outside the Zepa enclave? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: We should be very precise about our language here. You raised the -- my -- what you termed reluctance to use evacuation earlier with respect to the women and children, and I'm going to suggest, General, that evacuation is completely inappropriate here. We should use the word "escape." And according to this information - and I congratulate my colleague Mr. Bezruchenko; this seems to be very serious research that he did - of course, he and I couldn't have known any of this at the time, but this is quite interesting detail, and it suggests, as I testified earlier, that the bulk of the men of Zepa survived and escaped. Had they not succeeded and had they fallen to custody of the Serb forces, well, fate might have dealt them a much less kind result.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since we don't have much time, can you just answer my question. This is a report based on Muslim sources. According to this report, was a single soldier left within the Zepa enclave? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to this report and the lengthy paragraph that you took the time to read, it would appear that they fled and left and escaped.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now have D111. Thank you. This is D111. It contains mostly of names and numbers. Those are the persons who crossed over to Serbia. I would now like e-court to move from one page to another, going from page to page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And while they're doing that, I'm going to ask the question -- the witness the following: Did the UNPROFOR after the end of its affairs in Zepa make contact with Serbia in order to see what happened to the soldiers who surrendered to Serbia? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That -- I don't know the answer to either. I believe that there were diplomats who were involved in that, and there was communication with Belgrade about that on the diplomatic side.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since Bezruchenko's report mention about 1.371 persons who left Zepa to Serbia and other locations, can you tell me, did you have any information on UNPROFOR visiting other locations besides Serbia in order to find out what happened to the soldiers who left the Zepa enclave and arrived at other zones and areas? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have that information. And that activity, of course, would be dependent on what had been reported to high levels in UNPROFOR from diplomats who would have had knowledge about what was going on in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Since we only have five minutes left, I would like you to tell us the following: When you and Mr. Bezruchenko proposed demilitarisation of Zepa, what exactly did you have in mind? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Trying to answer concisely and briefly, first of all, it was Mr. Harland and I who proposed that, and what we had in mind was a proposal to avert the final collapse of Zepa and avert what might be a military assault that would leave a lot of casualties and/or what transpired, which is the complete -- the mass movement of the population and all the potentials that go along with either of those. And so that's what we had in mind in terms of our objective. In terms of the way it was written, it was written quite mindful of the mindset of both the Serbs and the Bosnians, Bosniaks, Muslims, as you wish, and that what the crucial component was contained not in the terms of the agreement but in the communication that the UN would have with each side and that is specific consequences for the Bosnian/Bosniak side if they refused, and specific consequences for the Serb side if they refused.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have 65 ter 2438. Page 13 in English and 15 in Serbian. This is a report dated 19th of July, 1995, entitled, "Proposal for Demilitarisation of Zepa". I would like us to see the page containing actual recommendations. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So while I still have a few minutes left, I would like to ask you the following: Why did you, in this proposal, write that you would show this proposal first to the Muslim side, and then, if they agreed to it, only later to the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer precisely. Not because I don't want to, but because it's hard for me now to remember exactly what we were thinking. Probably, to hazard a thought about it, we thought it would be more likely that we would get a yes from the Bosnian side and that therefore it would be -- and plus we had -- the communication was easier, but I think probably what we were thinking, we would get a yes there. And that with a yes from one side, the prospects for the agreement ultimately getting a yes would be greater. Ultimately getting a yes from both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have page 2 so that we can see the threats directed at both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You say here that if the Serbian side does not accept negotiations, then pursuant to the relevant resolutions, enumerated by you, they would be open to the NATO air-strikes. I think that that's what you say in the last sentence of the last paragraph. Yes, now we can see it. That's the last paragraph in Serbian under "Recommendation and Authority," where you say: "Should the Bosnian government accept the agreement and the Bosnian Serbs refuse, Pale will be informed that ..." and then I skip a bit "... Pale will be subject to NATO air-strikes." So my question is: Why do you threaten with the NATO air-strikes if the VRS accepted to demilitarise the zone? And that was something that General Mladic talked about in February 1995 and also sent a letter to the UNPROFOR basically to the same effect. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD JOSEPH [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I could -- I don't know if -- it's probably not permitted, but what I would ask back to the witness is: Are we speaking about a point, and I believe we are, where Serb forces are now in Zepa? I think that's what we're speaking about. And I believe I testified yesterday that the previous agreement, Halilovic-Mladic, about demilitarisation had been completely superseded by events on the ground there in Zepa, also had been overtaken by the fact that Srebrenica had fallen just a couple of weeks prior. So we're talking about a completely different context here, General Tolimir. We're talking about a context in which your forces are already, I would presume at the time of this writing, inside the boundaries of the safe area. And what David and I are trying to do is come up with something at the last minute that could avert a potential catastrophe. So that's -- that would explain that. And the use of NATO air-power was already authorised by the security counsel, as you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Nyambe has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: I'm trying to go back to the question. The question was: "So my question is: Why do you threaten with the NATO air-strikes if the VRS accepted to demilitarise the zone? ... that was something ..." Okay we end there. I think that your answer falls short of answering that particular aspect in the context of your own proposal with Mr. Harland, at that point when you were drafting that proposal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And let me try to find the actual proposal and then fully answer your question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you allow me, while the witness is looking for the portion he's interested in, I would like to call a document. 1D609, and just to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No, no, no, please stop.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- show page 4 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No, no, no, these are the last minutes. We have a document on the screen and this question was related to this document. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I think the first page we just need to go back, just to verify where -- I don't know if he wants to start on the first page, but I think we're looking at the second page of the agreement, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We should do that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, let me try to answer your question. If you're wondering why -- or if I'm not being responsive to the accused's question of why we would, in our proposal, why would we incorporate the threat of NATO air-strikes for demilitarisation when the Serbs had already accepted demilitarisation, if that's the thrust of the question posed to me by the accused. Is that the thrust of the question posed to me by the accused?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: I think let's go back to the transcript to get the exact question asked by the accused. Right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And could we also have the relevant page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No, please wait. Now Judge Nyambe is putting a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Yes, you can find the question on page 75, lines 23 to 25, into 76, 1.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know how to access that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No, it's not possible. It should be read out again. The Registrar will try to put it on the screen. The sentence begins with: "So my question is: Why ..." This is page 75, line 23. It's on the screen now. Judge Nyambe is referring to this question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. So trying to -- my best to respond to the question why do David Harland and I threaten the Serbs with NATO air-strikes if the VRS accepted to demilitarise, I think we need the word "had" in there. If, I think, the accused is suggesting "had," if the -- I think, if I understand the question correctly, what the accused is asking me is: Why do you threaten us with air-strikes when we had already accepted the demilitarisation? I think that's the question the accused is posing, and I can readily answer that. Because the circumstances had completely changed, and the Serbs had, in the past tense, accepted the condition of the continued existence, the conditioned presence of having this Muslim presence in Eastern Bosnia not far from the Serbian border. They had accepted that in the past under circumstances in -- under the condition that that area would be demilitarised. They had accepted that. Those circumstances had completely changed by July of 1995. The Serbs had, by their movements, the Serbs had gone into the safe area by force and were poised, had already begun, if my understanding of the sequence of events, were already attacking the village, forcing, and about to force the capitulation. So to be saying, Well, we accept it, why are you threatening us, we accept a demilitarisation. These circumstances have completely changed. There is no longer demilitarised -- or potentially demilitarised, in this context to the previous, because now we have Serb forces inside. Now there are Serb forces inside attacking or essentially poised to seise this territory. So the previous agreement was one which was written on the understanding that this territory would remain in Muslim hands. And now we are talking about a situation where Serb forces are there ready to vanquish the population that's there. And so it's in those circumstances that David and I, fearing the worst, fearing that this continued -- a final military assault could be a disaster and ultimately end up in a Srebrenica situation with a mass exodus of the population, as well with all that goes along with that, and so David and I in that context, knowing that this is what befalls, this is the fate that befalls this area, are saying, What could possibly avert that? How could we possibly avert that? Okay, we know it's very important for the Serbs to get this place really and truly demilitarised. Okay. We offer them that and we tell -- same with the Bosnian side, and we have this very short agreement, very clear, very serious and to the point about that, and we say to each side, Here it is, here you go, last chance; and if you don't accept Bosnians, here are the consequences for you; and if you don't accept Serbs, here are the consequences for you. And that's it. And then the one who doesn't accept, we know who's at fault. If it is accepted, we have potentially averted a catastrophe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Do you recall the date of your draft?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't recall the date. But I think it's -- it's incorporated, I believe, in the document of the 19th of July. But that's my resorting to these reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you indeed as well. We have to adjourn. We are very late now, and I apologise to the staff, the interpreters, court recorder, and all the other staff present here. We have to adjourn. And for your final questions, you may continue tomorrow, Mr. Tolimir. We resume tomorrow in the afternoon in this courtroom at 2.15. We adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 3rd day of March, 2011, at 2.15 p.m.
